analysis.one_liner: Requires safety review, manufacturing standards, and warning labels for dietary supplements.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote; it died in the Energy and Commerce Committee with 1 sponsor and 4 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have defined dietary supplements as a category of food, but subjected their ingredients to a new safety rule: an ingredient would be presumed unsafe unless it had a federal regulation, was scientifically proven safe, or was already in common use before August 1993 pending a government review. It would have required manufacturers to follow government-set quality-control and good-manufacturing standards, put expiration dates and adverse-effect warnings on labels, and required makers, distributors, and retailers to alert health officials when they had reason to believe a product was unsafe. It also directed NIH to expand research on supplements.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who take vitamins, minerals, and herbal products. The bill would have given the government the power to review the safety of supplement ingredients before and after sale, require labels to warn about dangerous dose levels and risks to children and the elderly, and guarantee that a bottle contains what the label says.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who take vitamins and herbal supplements

how_it_helps.text: An ingredient would be deemed unsafe unless it had a federal safety regulation, was generally recognized as safe by qualified experts through scientific procedures, or was grandfathered pending a mandatory government safety review begun within 60 days of enactment [S3].
The Secretary would have to write good-manufacturing-practice and quality-control rules so that a supplement actually provides what its label claims and is made to prevent adulteration [S3].

Labels would have to carry an expiration date and, where appropriate, warnings about the dose level at which a supplement can cause adverse effects and which populations, including children and the elderly, may be affected [S3].
Manufacturers, distributors, and retailers who had reason to believe a supplement or ingredient was adulterated or misbranded would have to promptly notify the Secretary [S3].
NIH would have to expand dietary supplement research, authorized at $10 million for fiscal 1994 plus sums for 1995-1997 [S3][S2].

analysis.who_pays: Dietary supplement manufacturers and ingredient suppliers, who would bear the cost of safety petitions, government review, manufacturing upgrades, and new labeling. Some products and ingredients might not survive the safety review, and compliance costs could be passed to consumers through higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The premarket safety-review structure mirrors the food-additive system: every new ingredient would need either a scientific consensus or a government petition process, which could delay or keep off the market products many consumers want, and those compliance costs would likely be passed on in prices [S3].

Ingredients already sold before August 1993 could stay on the market based on 'common use' rather than scientific testing while awaiting review, a weaker safety standard than the bill applies to new ingredients [S3].

The bill relies on the Secretary to write all the key rules — quality factors, manufacturing practices, warning labels, petition procedures — so its real-world effect would depend entirely on later regulations that could be slow or weakened [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-protection gains are real but run through a heavy regulatory machine. For everyday supplement users, the safety reviews, manufacturing standards, and adverse-effect warnings address a genuine gap — supplements could be sold with little proof of safety or purity. The costs fall on an industry that in the early 1990s was fighting hard against exactly this kind of FDA oversight, and some products would have become more expensive or disappeared. On balance, the bill was designed to shift the risk of unsafe products from consumers back to manufacturers, at the price of slower access to new products.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 1995 without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Cardiss Collins introduced the bill on August 6, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5][S1].
On September 3, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; no further committee action appears in the record [S5].
Four House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no member of the other party did [S4].
The sponsor gave introductory remarks on the floor when the bill was introduced and again in November 1993, but the bill never reached a markup or floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dietary supplement makers were better off because the bill died: no safety-review requirement, manufacturing rules, or warning-label mandates took effect, and the following year Congress enacted a very different law, the 1994 dietary supplement law, that largely left pre-1994 ingredients on the market without this kind of safety proof. Consumers who take supplements kept a marketplace with weaker government safety oversight.

for.name: Rep. Cardiss Collins
for.role: Sponsor; member of the Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks on the House floor in August and November 1993, and referred it to the committee on which she served

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; it was referred to the health subcommittee on September 3, 1993, and saw no markup or vote for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Dietary supplement industry
against.role: Manufacturers and sellers of vitamins, minerals, and herbal products
against.what_they_did: Conducted a broad campaign against FDA regulation of supplements in this period, favoring instead the 1994 law that largely preserved pre-market freedom for supplement ingredients

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill died in a committee controlled by the same party, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Dietary supplement manufacturers and ingredient suppliers
industries.note: The bill would have subjected their ingredients to presumed-unsafe-until-proven-safe review, government manufacturing and quality standards, warning labels, and mandatory notification of suspected problems. In the actual outcome, the industry kept a marketplace where ingredients need not be proven safe before sale, and the 1994 law enacted instead largely preserved that arrangement.
Retailers would have shared a legal duty to notify health officials when they had reason to believe a product was adulterated or misbranded, a compliance obligation the bill's defeat erased.
